Reproductive output in the Common potoo (Nyctibius griseus) is exceptionally low, even by the standards of tropical caprimulgiforms. Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and field records consistently indicate only one clutch is produced each year [F_R_i = one clutch is produced each year]. This translates to a remarkably slow reproductive tempo that likely reflects the energetic constraints of a sit-and-wait foraging strategy. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period for a caprimulgiform (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), incubation is a protracted affair, demanding sustained parental commitment. The newly laid eggs themselves have an initial weight that has been estimated at approximately 29.3 grams [Ww0 = approximately 29.3 grams], a value derived from the size-adjusted expectation for a species that occupies this particular niche. This modest initial egg investment is consistent with the production of a single, relatively large egg that must sustain the developing embryo through an extended incubation period in a thermally demanding environment.

The incubation period for Nyctibius griseus is carefully orchestrated around thermal conditions. To promote optimal development, eggs are typically maintained at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during incubation, a value that aligns with the optimal artificial incubation temperature for many avian species. Under these controlled thermal conditions, hatching occurs after an age at birth of approximately 31.5 days [ab = approximately 31.5 days] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This extended developmental timeline is a key feature of the potoo's life history, allowing for the thorough formation of a semi-precocial chick that is well-equipped to face the challenges of its arboreal habitat immediately after emergence. The consistent maintenance of this temperature is critical; fluctuations could delay development or compromise hatchling viability, underscoring the importance of stable brooding behavior by the attending adult. The careful thermoregulation of the egg by the parent bird is therefore an essential component of successful reproduction for this species.

The growth and development of the altricial nestling proceeds under the continued influence of ambient thermal conditions. During the period when the chick is most actively growing, typically maintained at an environmental temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the nestling reaches the critical developmental milestone of fledging at 43.5 days after hatching [tx = 43.5 days after hatching]. This timing marks the achievement of sustained flight and independence from the nest site, although the young bird may remain in close proximity to the parental territory for some time thereafter. The relatively rapid progression to fledging, when considered against the total lifespan, reflects a strategy that minimizes the window of vulnerability in the nest. During this period, the chick undergoes a rapid transition from a downy, stationary occupant to a fully feathered, volant juvenile capable of evading predators and securing its own food. This developmental pace is typical for a tropical bird that must balance rapid growth with the energetic demands of feather production.

Sexual maturity in the Common potoo is not achieved quickly, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes survival over rapid turnover. Under the same metabolic thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty for Nyctibius griseus is approximately 130.5 days [tp = approximately 130.5 days]. This milestone marks the onset of gonadal maturation and the beginning of reproductive potential, though the young adult may not secure a territory or a mate immediately. The delay to first breeding is considerably longer; the time since birth at first brood for a successful individual is 640 days since birth [tR = 640 days since birth] under optimal conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This substantial gap between physiological maturity and actual first reproduction suggests that social factors, such as competition for nesting sites or high-quality foraging perches, create a significant bottleneck for young birds entering the breeding population. This extended juvenile phase is a common feature among long-lived tropical birds.

Adult body size exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, which is a notable feature of its life history. Female potoos reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 180 grams [Wwi = approximately 180 grams], whereas males attain a considerably larger adult body mass, reaching around 242 grams [Wwi = around 242 grams]. This reversal of the typical avian size dimorphism, where females are often the larger sex, is intriguing and may be linked to differences in territorial behavior or social roles during the breeding season. The larger male mass may confer an advantage in defending nesting territories or in the courtship displays that precede mating. Accounting for this dimorphism is critical when modeling population dynamics or estimating energetic demands, as the metabolic requirements of a 242 gram male are substantially different from those of a 180 gram female. The lifespan of Nyctibius griseus, based on comparisons with related species such as the tawny frogmouth (Podargus strigoides) and measured under the same thermal conditions (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), is estimated to be around 40 years [am = around 40 years]. This impressive longevity, combined with the extremely low annual reproductive output of a single egg per year, firmly places the Common potoo among the most slow-lived, K-selected of all bird species. These life-history traits make the species particularly vulnerable to any increase in adult mortality.
